openers.subsidies-information-and-voluntary-appr: Governments do not only tax polluters and cap their emissions; they also pay, inform and persuade. A {{ref:nature-pol-205}} passes taxpayers' money to people or firms to support them or encourage some activity, and support for coal, oil and gas is among the largest. Other tools work through information: an {{ref:nature-pol-186}} tells shoppers about a product's environmental impact, and voluntary standards let producers show good practice. Nudges change how choices are presented, steering behavior without forcing it. Behind many of these tools sits a question of caution: how to act on possible harm when scientific knowledge is still incomplete.

nature-pol-205.title: Subsidies: paying people to do more of something
nature-pol-205.text: Many governments spend several percentage points of their GDP on subsidies, year after year. A subsidy is government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses, to support them or to encourage some activity. The word can also cover support from NGOs or international organizations. Subsidies come in many shapes. Some are direct spending, such as the payments governments may hand out in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity. Others are tax incentives, cheap loans, price support, or goods and services the government provides. Some do clear environmental good. Governments that subsidize rail and bus transport cut congestion and pollution compared with cars. But the tool cuts both ways. Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences, a theme that runs through this chapter.

nature-pol-201.title: The precautionary principle: caution before proof
nature-pol-201.text: When a new technology might cause harm and the science is still incomplete, who has to prove what? The precautionary principle answers by favoring caution and review first. Policy makers often use it when a decision might cause harm and conclusive evidence is not yet available. The English term is generally thought to come from the German Vorsorgeprinzip, adopted in the 1970s in response to forest decline and sea pollution. The principle has two core ideas. First, it shifts the burden of proof: whoever proposes an activity must show it will not, or is very unlikely to, cause significant harm. Second, the response should be proportionate to the risk and to the cost and feasibility of acting. It is not one fixed rule. One study found 14 different formulations in treaties and declarations. The EU's policies on the environment must be based on it, along with prevention, fixing damage at source and the {{ref:nature-pol-095}}. It is typically applied to climate change, new organisms such as GMOs, public health threats and the long-term effects of new technologies. Supporters see it as needed caution under uncertainty. Critics call it vague, self-cancelling, unscientific and an obstacle to progress.

nature-pol-186.title: Ecolabels: the environment on the package
nature-pol-186.text: Germany's Blue Angel, launched in 1978, was the world's first ecolabel. Today the Ecolabel Index counts 456 of them in 199 countries across 25 industry sectors. An ecolabel tells shoppers about a product's environmental impact. Ecolabels are voluntary, whereas green stickers are required by law. Some measure pollution or energy use with scores or units; others certify that a set of minimum practices was followed. Through certification, a farm, forest, fishery or mine can show it meets a standard and sell its products as certified. Labels put market pressure on industries to cut their impact, by linking products to the wishes of informed consumers. Trust is the weak spot. Some manufacturers have set up 'rubber stamp' labels to make products look greener than they are ({{ref:nature-nbs-075}}), so shoppers cannot take every label at face value.

nature-pol-184.title: Sustainability standards: voluntary rules for good practice
nature-pol-184.text: About 40% of global coffee production is certified, and about 15–20% of cocoa and tea production meets major sustainability standards. These standards are voluntary guidelines that producers, traders and retailers follow to show good environmental, social, ethical and food-safety practices. More than 400 exist around the world. A standard is usually written by stakeholders and experts in a sector and lists practices, such as how a crop should be grown sustainably. Certification checks that a business meets it. Traceability then follows certified goods along the supply chain, often ending in a label for shoppers. The standards grew up where national and global laws were weak but consumers and campaign groups demanded action. Some set a high bar and work with top performers; others aim to remove the worst practices across most of an industry. They also differ in whether a first, second or third party does the checking, and whether certified and uncertified material may be mixed. Researchers still debate how effective these schemes are and how they are governed.

nature-pol-221.title: Fair trade: a better deal for producers in poorer countries
nature-pol-221.text: Coffee is the most established fair trade commodity, but the movement also covers handicrafts, cocoa, wine, sugar, fruit, flowers and gold. Fair trade is a trade arrangement meant to help producers in developing countries get sustainable and fair conditions, by paying higher prices and raising social and environmental standards. The current movement took shape in Europe in the 1960s. Sales only took off once Fairtrade certification labels arrived. Fairtrade labeling uses independent audits of producers and traders, and its most distinctive feature is a guaranteed minimum price. In 2011 more than 1.2 million farmers and workers in over 60 countries took part in Fairtrade International's system. Some propose direct trade, which skips the overhead of certification, as an alternative.

nature-pol-192.title: Energy subsidies: who pays for cheap power
nature-pol-192.text: In 2020 the International Renewable Energy Agency tracked some $634 billion in energy subsidies, around 70% of them for fossil fuels. About 20% went to renewable power, 6% to biofuels and just over 3% to nuclear. An energy subsidy is a government measure that keeps energy prices below market levels for customers, keeps them above market levels for suppliers, or cuts their costs. It can be a direct cash payment or indirect support: tax exemptions, price controls, trade restrictions and limits on market access. Other forms include public research, cheap government services, demand guarantees, and failing to charge for external costs such as pollution. Which source gets the most support can affect the environment. Early support for solar power by the United States and Germany helped bring renewable energy to market and cut emissions worldwide. Because energy policies are interconnected across countries, regulating subsidies at the {{ref:nature-pol-007}} is often seen as necessary.

nature-pol-197.title: Fossil fuel subsidies: public money for coal, oil and gas
nature-pol-197.text: Under a narrow definition, fossil fuel subsidies totaled around $725 billion in 2024, 0.6% of global GDP, or up to $900 billion. Under a broader one they reached $6.7 trillion, 5.8% of GDP. They are any government action that lowers the cost of producing coal, oil or gas energy, raises producers' prices or lowers consumers' prices. Most of the money supports oil and natural gas. Most are consumption subsidies, such as lower sales tax on home-heating gas, or production subsidies, such as tax breaks for oil exploration. Broad definitions also count letting fuel users pollute the air and warm the climate without paying, an unpriced {{ref:nature-found-031}}. In effect these subsidies act as a negative carbon price. They use government money that could be spent on other things. And they are poorly aimed: economists agree the rich get most of the absolute benefit, since the poorest people usually do not own cars. The human cost is large. Subsidies are estimated to cause hundreds of thousands of deaths from air pollution each year. Removing them would cut those health risks and greatly reduce global carbon emissions.

nature-pol-234.title: Sustainable procurement: buying for the whole life cycle
nature-pol-234.text: Public spending averages 12% of GDP in OECD countries and up to 30% in developing countries, which gives governments enormous purchasing power. Firms have similar clout: purchases can exceed 50% of a company's expenses, and over 80% in retail, electronics and cars. Sustainable procurement puts that power to work. It means buying goods, services and works in a way that gives value for money over the whole life cycle ({{ref:nature-acct-050}}), while also benefiting society and staying within the environment's limits. Procurement has traditionally weighed only price and quality; the sustainable kind adds the third-party effects of buying decisions. It favors renewable or recycled materials and less waste, and checks suppliers for pollution or harm to habitats. It need not cost more. Sustainable options often cost about the same, and even pricier ones can save money through lower energy, water and waste costs over their life.

nature-pol-194.title: Extended producer responsibility: makers pay for the waste
nature-pol-194.text: In a 1990 report to the Swedish environment ministry, Thomas Lindhqvist first formally put forward a simple idea: make manufacturers pay for what becomes of their products. Extended producer responsibility, or EPR, holds producers responsible for environmental costs across a product's whole life cycle, mainly the cost of dealing with it as waste. The logic is that brand owners control product design, so they are best placed to cut toxicity and waste. Producers who pay end-of-life costs are pushed to design greener products. EPR can take the form of reuse, buyback or recycling programs, and producers may pay a producer responsibility organization to handle used products. Unlike product stewardship, which shares responsibility along the chain, it puts the cost of recycling into the product price and relieves local governments. The deposit-refund system is described as based on its principles. In Germany, packaging use per person fell from 94.7 kg to 82 kg between 1991 and 1998 after EPR was adopted, a reduction of 13.4%. A drawback is the administrative burden of rules that differ between countries and waste streams.

nature-pol-200.title: Nudges: steering choices without forcing them
nature-pol-200.text: More consumers chose renewable electricity when it was offered as the default option. That is a nudge at work. Nudge theory, from behavioral science, holds that changing how choices are presented, the {{ref:nature-econ-045}}, can steer behavior without forcing anyone. A nudge alters the setting so that fast, automatic thinking favors the desired choice. That sets it apart from education, legislation or enforcement. Nudges are small, cheap changes; techniques include defaults, social proof and making an option more noticeable. The 2008 book Nudge by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein made the idea popular. In tourism, nudges led people to reuse towels, choose more sustainable hotels and offset their carbon voluntarily. Governments use 'nudge units', such as the British Behavioural Insights Team set up in 2010. Whether nudges really work is disputed. A 2021 meta-analysis found nudging effective, with moderate {{ref:nature-econ-241}}. A later correction for that bias found no evidence of an effect.

nature-pol-213.title: The Common Agricultural Policy: Europe's farm support
nature-pol-213.text: Butter mountains and wine lakes: those were the nicknames for the huge surpluses the EU bought and stored under guaranteed prices. They came from the Common Agricultural Policy, the EU's farm policy, introduced in 1962. It runs a system of agricultural subsidies, risk management tools and other programs. Reforms have cut its share of the budget, from 73% in 1985 to 37% in 2017, and added rural development. The 'Agenda 2000' reforms split it into two pillars: production support and rural development. Many interests have criticized it since its start, and even the European Commission acknowledges its defects. Critics say it creates artificially high food prices, helped by import tariffs estimated at 18–28%. Because it has rewarded higher output, larger farms have gained far more from subsidies than smaller ones. A 2024 study reported that 80% of its subsidies in 2013 supported emissions-intensive animal products.

nature-pol-207.title: What a subsidy does to a market
nature-pol-207.text: A subsidy shifts the supply or demand curve to the right by the amount of the subsidy ({{ref:nature-econ-360}}). Which curve moves matters. A demand subsidy tends to raise prices, while a supply subsidy can lower them. In a competitive market, a subsidy pushes supply beyond the equilibrium quantity, the point where supply meets demand. The result is {{ref:nature-econ-345}}: the amount by which the subsidy's cost exceeds its gains, which grows with the subsidy's size. The effects cross borders. Subsidized goods sold abroad lower world prices, hurting producers in poorer countries and causing trade tensions. In 2019 the OECD urged countries to use more environmental taxation and to phase out agricultural subsidies and environmentally harmful tax breaks.

nature-pol-208.title: Perverse subsidies: support that harms twice over
nature-pol-208.text: In 2005 US farmers received $14 billion in agricultural subsidies, and EU farmers $47 billion. Farm subsidies like these often fuel environmental damage, deforestation and overfishing. Perverse subsidies are those whose effects are clearly and significantly harmful both to the economy and to the environment. A subsidy rarely starts out perverse. It can become so if it is not withdrawn after reaching its goal. Perverse subsidies drain budgets away from priorities such as conservation, education and health. They cause resource overuse and pollution, and tend to benefit the rich at the expense of the poor. And they are hard to remove, because they become 'locked' into society through bureaucratic roadblocks and institutional inertia.

nature-pol-237.title: Tax incentives: encouraging activity through the tax code
nature-pol-237.text: The hybrid vehicle tax credit is a typical tax incentive: a part of tax policy that encourages a particular economic activity by lowering the tax owed. For individuals, incentives include deductions, exemptions and credits. Conservation projects have traditionally drawn on public money that includes tax incentives. The record is mixed, though. Incentives aimed at single companies are generally seen as inefficient, costly, distorting and regressive, favoring the better-off. A 2020 study found some job gains from US state and local business incentives but no evidence of wider economic growth. Badly designed incentives can harm a government's finances.

nature-pol-224.title: Feed-in tariffs: guaranteed prices for clean power
nature-pol-224.text: As of 2019, more than 50 countries had feed-in tariff policies. A feed-in tariff speeds up investment in renewable energy by giving producers long-term contracts at a guaranteed, usually above-market price for the electricity they supply. It usually guarantees access to the grid and pays prices based on generating costs. Contracts typically run 15–25 years, and the price often falls over time to follow and encourage technology cost cuts. Different technologies get different prices; wind and solar PV, for example, get more per kWh than tidal power. A 2008 European Commission analysis found well-designed feed-in tariffs the most efficient and effective support for renewable electricity. They have a cost. Funded by a surcharge on bills, they added 6.88 cents/kWh for German households in 2017. Yet renewables can also lower spot market prices through the merit order effect, as happened in Spain, Denmark and Germany.

nature-pol-232.title: Pollution registers: the public's right to know
nature-pol-232.text: After the 1984 Bhopal disaster and the 1992 Rio conference, which affirmed people's right to know about toxic chemicals, several countries set up pollutant release and transfer registers. These systems collect and publish information on releases and transfers of hazardous substances from industrial and other facilities. The aim is to give nearby residents the same information as companies, since a level playing field matters for acceptance of permit decisions. A protocol to the Aarhus Convention requires its parties to set up such registers. That 2003 Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on them. The registers have a limit. Their data come mainly from facility questionnaires and remain the facilities' own estimates, even after official checks.

nature-pol-218.title: Environmental certification: choosing to be checked
nature-pol-218.text: Environmental certification is a voluntary form of environmental regulation. A company chooses to meet processes or goals set by a certification service, and most such services have a logo, commonly called an ecolabel, that certified products can carry. It is seen as a form of corporate social responsibility, letting firms reduce environmental harm by following external, measured objectives. Companies take it up to sell ethical products, improve their image, get on better with stakeholders and earn more profit. Independent checks of their green claims can also shield them from accusations of {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}. The whole system rests on demand. It only works if there are consumers willing to buy the resulting green products, and consumers may be willing to pay extra for ethically produced goods.

nature-pol-229.title: ISO 14000: international standards for environmental management
nature-pol-229.text: As of 2017, there were more than 300,000 ISO 14001 certifications in 171 countries. The ISO 14000 family is a set of international standards for environmental management systems, first issued by the International Organization for Standardization in March 1996. The standards help organizations cut their harm to air, water and land, comply with laws and keep improving. Like ISO 9000, they concern how a product or service is made rather than the product itself. ISO 14001 is the core standard. It sets out a framework for an environmental management system but no required level of environmental performance. The series is voluntary, and certification is done by third parties rather than by ISO itself. Firms that adopt it can cut waste, resource use and operating costs, and may gain a competitive advantage. Its predecessor was BS 7750, published in 1992 as the world's first environmental management system standard.

nature-pol-211.title: Forest certification: a label for responsibly managed wood
nature-pol-211.text: About 10% of the world's forest is under at least one certification program. Forest certification is a voluntary system that certifies wood and paper products as coming from forests managed responsibly under a particular standard. An independent body writes the standard, and independent auditors certify forest operations that meet it. Credible programs protect biodiversity and water quality, keep harvests sustainable and require prompt replanting. The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), a collaboration of environmental groups, forest companies and social interests, pioneered third-party certification in the early 1990s. With no single international standard, more than 50 scheme owners now offer certification. The two largest are the FSC and the PEFC, which covers about two-thirds of certified forest area. Critics such as Greenpeace and Jared Diamond question the rigor of rival standards, which some say logging companies set up to confuse consumers. The schemes defend their standards. Demand comes from publishers' paper commitments, green buying by governments, green building standards and laws against illegal logging.

nature-pol-209.title: Fishing subsidies: paying for too many boats
nature-pol-209.text: In 2002 the WWF estimated that about 75% of the world's major fisheries were overexploited. Fishing subsidies help explain why. They are government support for fishing: direct aid to fishers, loans, tax breaks, infrastructure and price support. These subsidies expand fleets and catches, favoring large-scale operations over small-scale fishers. Together they keep marine fisheries overfished and overcapitalized, holding more boats and gear than the fish can sustain.

nature-pol-206.title: Direct or indirect, production or consumption: sorting subsidies
nature-pol-206.text: Subsidies are sorted in three ways: direct or indirect, production or consumption, and broad or narrow. Direct subsidies are cash outlays to a specific person or household, such as cash grants. Indirect ones include tax breaks and low-interest loans. Production subsidies help suppliers expand output by offsetting costs, while consumption subsidies lower the price consumers pay. Consumption subsidies are most common in developing countries, for basics such as food, water, electricity and education. Broad subsidies are hard to identify and include non-monetary support. Environmental externalities, harms no one pays for, are the most common type.

nature-pol-220.title: EMAS: the EU's scheme for environmental management
nature-pol-220.text: The European Commission developed the Eco-Management and Audit Scheme, or EMAS, in March 1993. It is the EU's voluntary environmental management instrument, open to any type of organization worldwide. It helps organizations assess, manage and keep improving their environmental performance. Registering involves an environmental review, policy, program, management system, internal audit and a public environmental statement. Only accredited independent verifiers supervised by government bodies may validate those statements. Since 2010, registered organizations must report indicators on energy, materials, water, waste, biodiversity and emissions.

nature-pol-226.title: Green industrial policy: governments growing clean industries
nature-pol-226.text: German green industrial policy helped build a renewable energy industry employing over 371,000 people, double the jobs of 2004. Green industrial policy is government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting {{ref:nature-found-045}} and moving toward a low-carbon economy. The case rests on hard beginnings. Green industries such as renewable energy face high costs and risks, so they need public support until they become commercially viable. New sustainable technologies cannot compete at once with existing ones, because of {{ref:nature-pol-038}}, so governments nurture technological niches. Without government intervention, the market is unlikely to move to a low-carbon economy on its own. Subsidies for a targeted sector are the most common form. Other tools include R&D funding, tax credits, feed-in tariffs, mandates and green buying by governments.

nature-pol-231.title: The Inflation Reduction Act: America's biggest climate law
nature-pol-231.text: The Inflation Reduction Act, a 2022 United States law, is the largest federal legislation ever to address climate change, mainly through tax credits and grants for clean energy. According to the CBO and JCT, it invests $783 billion in energy security and climate provisions. Consumers get 10 years of tax credits for heat pumps, rooftop solar and efficient electric heating and cooling. It also created a $27 billion green bank, the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, to finance smaller regional green banks. After the act, Rhodium Group raised its forecast of 2030 US emission cuts from 17–30% to 29–42% below 2005 levels.

nature-pol-233.title: The Toxics Release Inventory: America's pollution register
nature-pol-233.text: The 1984 Bhopal disaster prompted Congress to create the Toxics Release Inventory in 1986, under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. It is a public US database of toxic chemical releases and waste management activities reported by industrial and federal facilities. For most listed chemicals, a facility must report if it makes 25,000 pounds, or processes or uses 10,000 pounds, a year. Reports cover releases to air, water and land, and amounts of waste sent off-site.

nature-pol-198.title: Counting fossil fuel subsidies: why the totals differ
nature-pol-198.text: In 2021 the UK government said it did not subsidize fossil fuels under the IEA definition, while others said it did under the OECD definition. Which definition to use is disputed, and with it whether some countries subsidize fossil fuels at all. Estimates add up government payments, compare domestic prices with world prices, and sometimes count health and climate damage. Counting those unpriced externalities makes IMF estimates far larger than those using OECD and International Energy Agency definitions. One IMF paper found underpricing of local air pollution was the largest part of global subsidies, at 42%, followed by global warming costs at 29%. The fiscal cost of government support for fossil fuels was 1.1 trillion USD in 2023, 90% of it tied to consumption.

nature-pol-246.title: Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters
nature-pol-246.text: Grandfathering gives out emission permits for free, according to how much each firm emitted in the past. It can create perverse incentives. A firm that cuts its emissions sharply may receive fewer permits later. Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits. The EU's trading scheme gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition. Free allocation is complex, and it encourages {{ref:nature-pol-042}}, the pursuit of favors from government, and pressure on officials ({{ref:nature-pol-034}}).

nature-pol-264.title: Water trading: markets for the right to use water
nature-pol-264.text: Chile's 1981 Water Code made the right to use water ({{ref:nature-res-168}}) freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial. Water trading is the buying and selling of water access entitlements between willing sellers and buyers. A seller holds rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more. Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more productive uses: urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers. The older first-in-time system of prior appropriation led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology. Water is a {{ref:nature-econ-610}}, but once rights make its use rival and excludable, it behaves like a private good. It is still no standard commodity. Supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin. Trades can also harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller. Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.

nature-pol-278.title: Market design: engineering the rules of exchange
nature-pol-278.text: Some markets are built on purpose. Market design is the branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange: who gets what, and by what procedure. Its aim is to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes. It is closely related to {{ref:nature-econ-008}} and auction theory. Alvin Roth pioneered applications in labor-market matching, organ transplantation and school choice. He and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel prize for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design. Auction theory supplies results such as the {{ref:nature-econ-009}}: with independent private values, sealed first-price and second-price auctions bring the same expected revenue.
